Predict From a Fitted Model

Source: R/predict.R
predict.StatmodFit.Rd

Predicts from a fitted model: any one of the distribution's parameters, any of its moments, every parameter or linear predictor at once, or a new observation of the response, at the fitting data or at new data, with standard errors and intervals on request.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'StatmodFit'
predict(
  object,
  what = "parameter",
  newdata = NULL,
  se = FALSE,
  level = 0.95,
  random = "conditional",
  interval = confidence_interval(),
  vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(),
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A StatmodFit().

what

What to predict: a parameter's name, optionally prefixed "link:"; a moment's name; "parameter" (the default) or "link"; or "response", which requires interval = prediction_interval() and is the only value that this interval accepts. An unrecognized name signals an error listing what is available.

newdata

A data frame, or NULL for the fitting data. It needs the variables of the equations that are read: where what names one parameter and interval is confidence_interval(), the variables that only the other equations use may be absent. It does not need the response, except that a moment or a prediction interval of a binomial fitted with cbind() reads the number of trials from it. For a model with a structural term, rows that all carry the response are read as a series of their own, and rows without it continue the fitted series. A data frame with no rows signals an error.

se

TRUE to report the standard error and an interval as well. The default is FALSE. A moment has no standard error, and se = TRUE with a moment signals an error. group_interval() sets it to TRUE, and prediction_interval() does not read it, because its result carries its own se column.

level

The interval's level, 0.95 by default, a single number strictly between 0 and 1. It is read wherever an interval is returned: with se = TRUE, with group_interval() and with prediction_interval(), which gives its interval without se.

random

How a modelterms7::random() term is read: "conditional" (the default) with each group's own estimated effect, so a level that is absent from the fitting data signals an error; "zero" with every effect at zero, the typical group; "marginal" averaged over the prior that the fit estimated, the population average \(E_b[h^{-1}(\eta + z^\top b)]\). A single string applies to every such term; a character vector named by the terms' keys sets the mode term by term, and the terms that it does not name stay conditional. See the section on new groups.

interval

An interval object that selects the uncertainty that the interval describes. confidence_interval() (the default) gives the interval of the parameter, the predictor or the moment from the uncertainty of the estimates; group_interval() gives the interval of the parameter of a new group; prediction_interval() gives the interval of a new observation of the response, and takes the predictive distribution as its argument (predictive = pred_averaged(), pred_plugin() or pred_bootstrap()). A character string is rejected with an error. See predict_intervals and predictive_distributions.

vcov_type

A vcov_method object that selects the variance convention of vcov.StatmodFit(): bayesian_vcov() (the default), frequentist_vcov() or unconditional_vcov(), which also accounts for the estimated smoothing parameters. It is read where se is TRUE, with group_interval(), and with prediction_interval() holding pred_averaged(), and a value other than the default signals an error elsewhere. The unconditional variance differs most from the others in a band around a penalized term, since a smoothing parameter moves the fitted values. The conventions are compared at vcov_method.

...

Not used. Any argument signals an error that names it.

Value

With se = FALSE, a numeric vector with one value per row of newdata (of the fitting data where newdata is NULL) when what names one quantity, and a named list of such vectors for "parameter" and "link".

With se = TRUE, a data frame with columns fit, se, lower and upper in place of each vector, or, for "parameter" and "link", a named list of such data frames, one per parameter. se is NA for an observation whose predictor reads a coefficient that has no variance.

With prediction_interval(), a data frame with columns fit (the predictive median), se (the predictive standard deviation, NA where it does not exist), lower and upper, all NA for a row whose predictor reads a coefficient that has no variance.

Quantities that can be predicted

what takes

a parameter's name

"mu", "sigma" or "alpha", whatever the family calls them. A parameter is available for every family, because the model fits it, and it exists even where a moment does not.

a moment's name

"mean", "variance", "std_dev", "skewness", "kurtosis". A moment is available where the family has one, and the result is NaN or NA where the moment does not exist. A Cauchy's mean is NaN, which is the correct answer for it. A moment has no standard error. For a binomial fitted with cbind(), a moment needs the number of trials of each row, so newdata has to carry the variables with which the response is written.

"parameter"

every parameter at once, as a named list. This is the default.

"link"

every linear predictor at once, before the inverse link.

"response"

the response itself, with interval = prediction_interval(), which it requires: its median and the ends of an interval in which a new observation falls. See the section on intervals.

A parameter's name may be prefixed by "link:" to return its predictor instead of its value, as "link:sigma".

The argument order departs from stats::predict()

There the second argument is newdata; here it is what. A statmod fit has several parameters and several moments, so choosing among them is the ordinary variation and predicting on new data is the occasional one.

A data frame passed second is detected, and the error names the argument order.

New data

New data is passed through each term's build_info, so a factor keeps the levels and contrasts with which it was fitted, a spline its knots, and a basis its reparametrization. The new frame supplies the values at which the terms are evaluated and does not change how they are built. Offsets are evaluated again at the new rows.

The new frame needs the variables of the equations that are read. Where what names one parameter and interval is confidence_interval(), the other equations are not read, and the variables that only they use may be absent from newdata. The response is not needed, except that a binomial fitted with cbind() reads the number of trials from it for a moment or a prediction interval.

A score-driven term is predicted past the series

The contribution of such a term at one row is the state that a recursion has reached, so new rows without the response continue the series instead of being read on their own. Each row is placed by its own time within its own group, and must come after every observed time of that group. A row that falls inside the observed series is rejected, since there the response is known and the filter has to be run, not continued. A group that is absent from the fitting data is rejected as well, and a term built without time cannot be continued, because the place of a row in the series is then its position in the data frame.

New rows that carry the response are a series of their own: the structural term is rebuilt on them with the fitted parameters, and they are read as the fitting rows are, including the standard errors. If the fitting data are passed as newdata, the result is that of predict(fit); this holds for a modelterms7::regime() term as well, whose prediction is the posterior-weighted predictor. A frame that carries the response on some rows only is rejected. A modelterms7::regime() term cannot be continued past the series, since what it reports at an observed row is a posterior over states.

Beyond the data the score sits at its conditional mean of zero, which the model's own definition guarantees, so the continuation is the deterministic recursion and involves no simulation.

A new group, and the typical one

A random-effect term predicts a group that is present in the fitting data with that group's estimated effect. A group that is absent from the fitting data has none, and what is put in its place depends on random. "zero" sets every effect of the term to zero, at every row, which is the prediction for the typical group (lme4's and glmmTMB's re.form = NA). "marginal" averages over the prior instead, \(E_b[h^{-1}(\eta_0 + z^\top b)]\), which is the population average. With an identity link the two agree for the mean; with a log link the marginal mean is \(\exp(\eta_0 + \sigma_b^2/2)\), and with a logit it is pulled towards one half. A moment is averaged by the law of total expectation and the variance adds the variance of the conditional mean, so a random effect on the scale enters the marginal variance of the response.

The average is a Gauss-Hermite product grid where every prior is Gaussian and there are at most three coordinates in all; adaptive quadrature against the prior's density (numericals7::quad_vec()) where the only effect set aside is one coordinate with a prior that is not Gaussian; and 10000 draws from the priors otherwise, on a seed of their own. A prior that is not Gaussian is integrated only where the inverse link is bounded: a Student t has no moment generating function, so under a log link the average does not exist, and such a request signals an error. Under a link whose predictor has a restricted domain (the square root and inverse links) the average does not exist either, since a Gaussian effect leaves the domain with positive probability; it is reported where that probability is below 1e-8 and is NA, with a warning, elsewhere. A term that shares a covariance with others through a label has no prior of its own, so "marginal" cannot average over it; it can be read "conditional" or set aside at "zero". The standard error of a marginal parameter is the delta method on the fixed part, conditional on the prior's scale.

A random effect written inside a term's subformula, such as nl(~ Asym / (1 + exp((xmid - age) / scal)), Asym ~ 1 + random(~ 1 | g)) or seg(t, psi ~ random(~ 1 | id)), is set aside by the same modes. Its key is the outer term's key, the parameter and the sub-term joined by "::", and an unnamed mode applies to it as well. The effect enters the term's parameter, and the term is not linear in it, so the term is evaluated at the effect's value rather than having its columns removed: "zero" evaluates it with the effect at zero at every row, and the delta method reads its Jacobian there. "marginal" averages the term's contribution, carried through the inverse link, over the nodes that the rule above builds for the priors set aside; a prior of another family signals an error. A predictor ("link") is the average of the predictors at the nodes. The standard error of a marginal parameter is the delta method of that average, whose gradient sums the design at each node, and its interval is the delta method's on the link scale carried through the link. group_interval() and prediction_interval() are not available for such an effect, and a standard error is not available where an average is taken over effects of both kinds.

Intervals and predictive distributions

The object given to interval selects the uncertainty that the interval describes: confidence_interval() the estimates alone, group_interval() the estimates and the effects of a new group, and prediction_interval() a new observation of the response. The topic predict_intervals compares the three and gives the formulas. A prediction interval holds a predictive object that sets how the estimation uncertainty enters: pred_averaged() (the default), pred_plugin() or pred_bootstrap(). The topic predictive_distributions compares them and states what each costs.

group_interval() and prediction_interval() are rejected for a multivariate family and for a model with a structural term. The structural term also rejects random = "zero" and random = "marginal": its level is a recursion read at the predictor, so setting a random effect aside would move the recursion as well.

A forecast's standard error, with se = TRUE, is only the uncertainty of the estimated parameters, carried by the delta method through the continued recursion, whose derivative is exact. A forecast also carries the uncertainty of the future scores, which the delta method does not reach, so the standard error and the interval leave it out, and a warning is issued for the equations that the continued filter reaches.

References

Harris, I. R. (1989). Predictive fit for natural exponential families. Biometrika, 76, 675–684.

See also

fitted.StatmodFit() for one parameter's fitted values, residuals.StatmodFit() for the matched diagnostic, vcov.StatmodFit() for the variance from which the standard errors are computed.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(60))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(60, sd = 0.4)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x | sigma ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)

# One parameter and one of the family's moments are predicted.
head(predict(fit, "mu"))
#> [1] 1.598797 1.804267 2.191116 2.837415 1.475789 2.818493
head(predict(fit, "variance"))
#> [1] 0.16546123 0.14306587 0.10879810 0.06885779 0.18051281 0.06978618

# The predictor of a parameter is returned instead of its value.
head(predict(fit, "link:sigma"))
#> [1] -0.8995092 -0.9722251 -1.1091307 -1.3378560 -0.8559768 -1.3311596

# For a Gaussian the mean is mu and the variance is sigma squared, and the
# moments of the fit return these values.
all.equal(predict(fit, "mean"), predict(fit, "mu"))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(predict(fit, "variance"), predict(fit, "sigma")^2)
#> [1] TRUE

# The result carries an interval as well.
head(predict(fit, "mu", se = TRUE))
#>        fit         se    lower    upper
#> 1 1.598797 0.07213967 1.457406 1.740188
#> 2 1.804267 0.05854267 1.689526 1.919009
#> 3 2.191116 0.04332413 2.106202 2.276029
#> 4 2.837415 0.06721771 2.705670 2.969159
#> 5 1.475789 0.08114458 1.316749 1.634830
#> 6 2.818493 0.06593854 2.689256 2.947730

# Every parameter is returned at once, on either scale.
str(predict(fit, "parameter"))
#> List of 2
#>  $ mu   : num [1:60] 1.6 1.8 2.19 2.84 1.48 ...
#>  $ sigma: num [1:60] 0.407 0.378 0.33 0.262 0.425 ...

# For a new group, the prediction is the typical one or the population
# average.
gg <- data.frame(g = factor(rep(letters[1:12], each = 10)),
                 x = rnorm(120))
gg$y <- rpois(120, exp(0.5 + 0.3 * gg$x + rnorm(12, sd = 0.6)[gg$g]))
fg <- statmod(y ~ x + random(~ 1 | g), distributions7::poisson_distrib(),
              gg)
new <- data.frame(g = "new", x = 0)
predict(fg, "mu", new, random = "zero")
#> [1] 1.593882
predict(fg, "mu", new, random = "marginal")
#> [1] 1.786905

# The calls return the interval of a new group's mean and of a new count
# from it.
predict(fg, what = "mu", newdata = new, random = "zero",
        interval = group_interval())
#>        fit        se     lower    upper
#> 1 1.593882 0.9711082 0.5944571 4.273577
predict(fg, what = "response", newdata = new, random = "zero",
        interval = prediction_interval(predictive = pred_plugin()))
#>   fit       se lower upper
#> 1   1 1.614653     0     6
predict(fg, what = "response", newdata = new, random = "zero",
        interval = prediction_interval())
#>   fit       se lower upper
#> 1   1 1.658936     0     6

# A name that the family does not have is rejected, and the message lists
# what is available.
try(predict(fit, "median"))
#> Error : 'median' is neither a parameter of this distribution nor a
#>   moment. The parameters are: mu, sigma.
#>   The moments are: mean, variance, std_dev, skewness, kurtosis.
#>   "parameter" and "link" give all of them at once.
